headline: A Sigstore bundle signed over an artifact's own bytes is verified, not just one wrapping an attestation.
summary: cosign sign-blob produces a bundle whose content is a signature over the artifact itself rather than a DSSE-wrapped statement about it. pki.sigstore.verifyBundle now reads that arm. The caller supplies the artifact, it is held to the hash the transparency-log entry records, and only then is the signature checked over its bytes.

Added: pki.sigstore.verifyBundle verifies a bundle carrying a message_signature. The caller passes the artifact as opts.artifact and the verifier hashes it: under the algorithm the Rekor entry names, compared against the hash that entry records, and then under the leaf certificate's key against the signature the bundle carries. The three happy-path bundles the Sigstore conformance suite publishes are the vectors, covering all three bundle media types and both shapes of verification material.

opts.artifact takes the artifact's bytes and nothing else. The digest a message_signature carries is covered by no signature, and the field's own definition states that a client must not use it to verify the signature, so there is no shape in which a caller hands over a digest instead: a hex string is refused at the door, and the digest bytes are refused where the artifact is compared against the log entry. A message_signature bundle with no opts.artifact is refused rather than verified from the digest it carries.

The digest the bundle states is checked against the one computed, when it is there. It is optional, and a bundle omitting it verifies with messageDigestChecked reporting false. Where it disagrees with the artifact the request is refused, and the verdict reports the digest this computed rather than the one the bundle claimed. It may name any of the five members the HashAlgorithm enum defines, the two SHA-3 members included: those are marked deprecated, which says a producer should not choose one rather than that a bundle carrying one is malformed, and this digest names its own algorithm independently of the one the log entry records. It may name the member by its name or by its number, since the JSON mapping states that a parser accepts both; the unspecified member is refused under either spelling, as is a number outside the enum. The entry's algorithm is a different field under a different enum and stays the three the Rekor schema lists.

The verdict has one shape for both content arms. contentType names the arm. The fields that carry a value report null where the arm has none: artifactDigest and digestAlgorithm on a DSSE bundle, and payload, statement, subjects, predicateType and predicate on a message signature. The fields that report whether a check ran stay boolean, so messageDigestChecked is false on a DSSE bundle exactly as predicateTypeChecked is false on a message signature. A caller reads the same fields either way rather than telling a missing key from a false one.

opts.identity and opts.ctLogs run on this arm as they do on the other, so a caller pins who signed and whether the signing certificate was public when it was issued, whichever content the bundle carries.
Changed: A hashedrekord entry may name the verifier as a public key rather than as a certificate. The Rekor field is documented as the public key that verifies the signature, which may also be an X509 code signing certificate carrying that key, so an entry writing the key itself is conforming; it binds when that key is the bundle leaf's, and an entry naming a different key does not bind. The armor says which form the entry wrote, so neither is guessed at from the bytes.

An option supplied on the options object's prototype is read as the option it is, which is how the unknown-option gate and the verdict already read it. Reading opts.artifact and opts.predicateType as own properties made an inherited artifact look missing on the arm that requires it, passed an inherited one over unread on the arm that refuses it, and let an inherited predicateType through that refusal and then be reported as checked by a verdict with no statement to check it against.

A transparency-log entry is read by its own kind and version together. The entry registry holds one row per kind and apiVersion, and each row states which content arm it may accompany, so a hashedrekord v0.0.2 body is refused as an unsupported version rather than read for v0.0.1 field names it does not carry, and an entry describing a DSSE envelope beside a message signature is refused rather than bound to it.

An option that belongs to the other arm is refused rather than ignored. opts.artifact on a dsse_envelope bundle and opts.predicateType on a message_signature are each an error, since an option read and passed over reads as a check that ran.
Fixed: A bundle given as an object holds its fields as values, and one reached through an accessor is refused rather than called. Values are taken from each property's descriptor, so nothing the caller wrote runs while the bundle is being read: a field cannot answer differently on a later read, and a field that computes its value cannot change the object being read. That last one is why calling nothing is the rule rather than reading once, since a getter on one property could delete another and leave a bundle carrying two content arms copied as one. pki.sigstore.parseBundle takes the same copy and returns it, so a caller reads back what was checked and the two verbs cannot answer differently about one bundle.

A bundle given as an object is copied into plain data before anything reads it, and each of its own properties is read exactly once. Its fields are the caller's own, and an accessor may answer differently each time, so a value could be checked in one place and a different one used in another. The transparency-log entry's canonicalizedBody was read separately by the three things that examine it, the binding that ties the entry to the signature and certificate, the inclusion proof folded to the signed tree root, and the signed entry timestamp; a field answering differently across those reads let one body be bound while a different one was proven, so a signature the log never recorded was attested by an authentic entry for something else and verifyBundle returned verified. The same shape reached the DSSE payload and signature, the inclusion proof's root and hashes, and the log time the certificate is checked at. A single read leaves no second observation to disagree with the first, so every check runs on data that cannot change under it, whichever field it reads and however many times. This affects both content arms and every version that shipped the DSSE one; a bundle given as JSON text was never affected, since parsing it yields fixed values. Object input now also carries the reader's size and depth caps.

The size of an object bundle is charged as the copy is built, so it is refused before the memory is allocated rather than after. Two shapes need this and a depth limit bounds neither: sharing one sub-object between two properties doubles the values a copy walks per level, so a few hundred bytes describes hundreds of millions of them, and a modest array of long strings is a handful of values holding tens of megabytes. Counting one byte per value plus the length of every string and key counts no more than the serialized form does, so nothing the size limit would have admitted is refused.

Nothing stands between the copy and the checks that run on it. The object path used to serialize the copy and read it back, which put a serializer on the path: one replaced after this package loads is read at the moment it is called, and one that drops a field would hand the checks a bundle carrying a single content arm where the copy holds two. The copy is plain data with its size and depth already charged while it was built, so it is not converted to text at all. The operations that decide what an object owns and what it holds are taken at load for the same reason, since replacing one of those alone empties the copy.

A bundle object holding a value JSON does not carry is refused. A function, a symbol, a bigint or a non-finite number anywhere in the structure means the object is not a bundle, and dropping one silently is how a bundle setting two content arms became a bundle setting one, which is a refusal turned into an acceptance. A field set to undefined is the exception and reads as absent, which is what an absent field means.

The fields that name a registry row are read for being strings before they are used as keys. A messageDigest algorithm, a log entry's kind and apiVersion, and a log entry's hash algorithm reached a lookup as whatever the bundle carried, so a value whose own conversion throws escaped as an untyped error out of a verb whose contract is that malformed input is refused with a typed one.
